script: NBA players who started the CRAZIEST retirement gigs! When Wayman Tisdale was a kid, his dad, a pastor in Tulsa, bought all three of his sons Mickey Mouse guitars, hoping at least one of them would pick up music. And Wayman was the one who got hooked. He started teaching himself bass guitar after falling in love with watching the bass players at his father's church, and he played there every single Sunday growing up because music was always his first love. But then his body had different plans for him. In junior high, Tisdale grew 24 inches and suddenly became one of the best basketball players in the States, which led him to the University of Oklahoma, where he became the first freshman ever named a First Team AP All-American, and then did it again as a sophomore and a junior. He still holds Oklahoma's all-time scoring record with 2,661 points, got drafted second overall in 1985 by the Indiana Pacers, and played 12 years in the NBA across three teams. And during all of this, he never once stopped playing bass, to the point where his college coach actually moved Sunday practices to the evening just so Tisdale could drive to Tulsa and play at his dad's church that morning. But here's what most people don't realize about his music career. His debut album dropped in 1995 while he was still on the Phoenix Suns roster, and it hit number four on the Billboard jazz chart. After he retired in '97, he went all in, and multiple albums hit number one on Billboard's contemporary jazz chart as he headlined festivals worldwide. Then, in 2007, he was diagnosed with bone cancer, and he kept performing even after losing part of his right leg. But on May 15th, 2009, Tisdale passed away at just 44 years old, only 12 years into the career he'd been waiting his whole life to fully chase.
